title: Agility and reaction
summary: How agility differs from change of direction, the levels of reaction training, solo and partner versions, and how to get the most from reaction work without a coach there.

p: Agility means moving or changing direction in response to a cue. That could be a ball coming at you, your opponent's racket, or a call that tells you which way. Change of direction means moving along a path you already know.
Tennis needs both. Braking and change of direction drills teach your body how to move. Reaction drills add when and which way.

In team sport studies, planned change of direction and agility keep showing up as separate skills. In one small trial with teenage Australian football players, small games cut decision time, but change of direction drills did not help reactive agility. A 2026 meta-analysis of speed and agility training also found no significant effect on reactive agility (low certainty), and all of this evidence is small and from other sports.
sections.callout: Know the path in advance? That's change of direction. A cue picks the path? That's agility.

sections.h: When the cue arrives sets the level
p: How hard a reaction drill is depends mostly on when the cue arrives. These four levels and the 16-week progression are the course's own rule, not a study result:
list: Planned: no cue, you know the path in advance. This is change of direction, not agility.
Simple reaction: the direction is known, only the start time isn't. For example, the Ball Drop Reaction Sprint.
Semi-reactive: the cue comes before your first step, while you're standing or split stepping, with 2 to 4 options. Most reaction drills in your programme are this kind.
Reactive: the cue comes while you're already moving. Your programme only gives you a small taste of this.
sections.callout: Over time the options go from 2 to 3 and 4, the cues go from pointing and colours to a shadow racket swing, and the cue comes a little later each time.

sections.h: Reaction drills in your court sessions
p: Your court sessions have a reaction part, after the sprints and brakes while your legs are still fresh.
list: Foundation: Ball Drop Reaction Sprint. Known direction, unknown timing.
Build: Point-Cue Shuffle Sprint. Two options, with the cue a little later each week.
Explosive: Racket-Cue Reaction Sprint. Three options, then tennis cues: a shadow forehand, backhand or drop shot.
Court transfer: Two-Cue Court Reaction. Two cues in each rep, with 3 and then 4 options.
sections.callout: In most reps: split step, see or hear the cue, go, brake and get back to the middle.

p: Every reaction drill has a version for when nobody's with you. The note on each drill tells you which one.
list: Wall: Wall Feed Reaction. Hit a tennis ball hard at a wall, split step and move to where it comes back. For three directions, hit it into the corner of the wall.
Ball drop: Self-Drop Drop-Step. Drop a ball from shoulder height behind you, turn and chase it. You pick the timing, so the reaction part is weaker.

Colour or direction calls: use a random cue app on your phone. After a random pause of 1 to 3 seconds it calls left, right or a colour. In the Colour-Call Cone Sprint, for example, you sprint to the cone of that colour.
sections.callout: Whenever you can, a partner beats the ball drop version.

sections.h: With a partner: parent, coach or friend
p: Every reaction drill has a partner version too. The partner should follow these rules:
list: Stand where the player can see you well. Say “ready” once and wait until they're in a ready position.
Before the cue, keep your face and body still and don't look at the side you picked.
Pick the side at random. Check a clock before each rep: an even second means left, an odd second means right.
Don't give a cue while the player is in the air or off balance.
If the player slips, stumbles or says something hurts, stop the drill.
sections.callout: People make patterns without noticing, so a player can learn to guess. Random picks are what keep the drill reactive. The clock rule is just one simple way to do it, not a tested method, and evenly paced reps can make it predictable.

p: 16 and over: when it's in your programme, the last two reaction reps in a court session are truly reactive. The second cue comes while you're still getting back to the middle (Called Court Pattern).

A partner by the net post calls a number: 1 forehand wide, 2 backhand wide, 3 forehand short, 4 backhand short. With no partner, use a cue app. If you have neither, do every rep as a Two-Cue Court Reaction.
This is only a taste. Full reactive training is more advanced work that comes later.
sections.warn: Under 16: every cue comes during the split step and every rep is a Two-Cue Court Reaction. This is the course's own safety rule, not a study result.

sections.h: Getting the most from reaction work without a coach
p: The see-and-decide part of agility can be trained, but the evidence still comes from small studies. These points help every rep really train your reaction:
list: Don't guess. Stay balanced with your weight on both feet until the cue comes. Moving before the cue means you didn't train your reaction.

Land your split step as you start to pick up the cue, not well before it. In one simulated tennis task, landing well before the usual response time gave a quick start but 7.8% misses, against 0.8% when players landed close to it.
Keep the cues random: a cue app, a partner using the clock rule, or throws that hit a different spot on the wall each time.
Eyes on the cue, meaning the ball or the partner's hand or racket, not the ground.
Went the wrong way? Don't twist on a planted foot. Brake over a few steps, then come back.
Take the full rest in your session so every rep is fast.
sections.callout: Train reaction with quality: random, fast reps, not lots of predictable ones.

p: Reaction drills only go in court sessions, not in the gym.
list: Court sessions: after the sprints and brakes.
Extra speed and agility sessions, if you have them: more reaction reps, for when you get to wide or short balls late.
The spider test has a set path. So it shows how fast you move around the court, not how well you react.
A training ladder isn't agility either. The lesson “Speed, braking and change of direction” explains why.
